title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a target value k, find the total number of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum exactly to k. Solve it with the prefix-sum and hash-map pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Subarray Sum Equals K (Prefix Sum with a Hash Map)
keyPoints: A subarray sum equals the difference of two prefix sums: prefix[i] - prefix[j] = k.
At each index, count how many earlier prefix sums equal prefix[i] - k using a hash map.
Seed the map with prefix value 0 mapped to count 1 (representing the empty prefix before the array).
Look up before inserting to avoid matching an element against itself.
This works with negatives and zeros where sliding windows fail.
Time is O(N) and space is O(N) for the hash map.

s1_definition.oneliner: Count earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k, using a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies.
s1_definition.profdef:
- This problem counts contiguous subarrays summing to exactly k, in an array with possible negatives.
- The **prefix sum** at index i is the sum of all elements from 0 to i.
- A subarray from j+1 to i sums to k when `prefix[i] - prefix[j] = k`, i.e., `prefix[j] = prefix[i] - k`.
- A **hash map** tracks how many times each prefix value has occurred.
- **Seed** the map with `{0: 1}` for the empty prefix; **look up before insert**.
- Time is **O(N)** and space is **O(N)**.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh walks through a sequence of daily net cash flows for a suspense account and counts how many continuous stretches netted exactly zero (a perfectly balanced stretch). He keeps a running total and remembers how often each total appeared. Whenever his current total minus the target has been seen before, each earlier occurrence marks the start of a qualifying stretch.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem counts contiguous subarrays summing exactly to k in an array that may contain negatives, and you solve it in linear time using a running prefix sum and a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies. A subarray sum equals the difference of two prefix sums, so a subarray ending at the current index sums to k when some earlier prefix equals the current prefix minus k. At each index, you add to your answer the count of times that value has appeared, then record the current prefix.

The two correctness linchpins are the seed and the ordering. Seed the map with prefix value 0 at count 1 to represent the empty prefix, so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted. Look up before inserting so you never match an element against itself.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this on the reconciliation team. They reviewed daily net cash flows for a suspense account and counted how many continuous stretches netted exactly a target amount, usually zero, because zero-netting stretches meant the account self-reconciled over that period. Flows could be positive or negative, so a sliding window was not applicable.

The senior-level insight is that the prefix-sum-with-hash-map technique is specifically the tool for signed arrays where sliding windows break. Knowing to reach for it the moment negatives appear is the real signal of experience.

Remember one sentence: at each index, look up prefix minus k in a frequency map of earlier prefix sums, seeded with {0: 1}, and the total lookups give the count of subarrays summing to k.
